A reproduction of the opening of the journal read this run gives the date heading September 15th and then, verbatim, BEGIN here. It is raining. I look out on the maple, where a few leaves have turned yellow, and listen to Punch, the parrot, talking to himself and to the rain ticking gently against the windows. So the two shipped sentences are the first two sentences of the first entry, in that order, ending at a full stop, and a second reference source independently reports that the journal runs from 15 September 1970 to 30 September 1971 and was published by W. W. Norton in 1973. Two small things, neither fatal. First, the printed text sets the first word in capitals, BEGIN here, which is the ordinary typographic convention for the opening words of a book and not the author's own capitals, so rendering it Begin here. is correct and not a silent change; but the editor should know the page looks different from the card. Second, the entry heading prints September 15th with no year, so the 1970 in the source line is supplied from the journal's known span rather than read off the page. It is correct, but it is an inference, and the note, which is currently empty, should say plainly that the entry heads itself September 15th and that the year comes from the journal's dated span. One caveat rather than a refutation: at twenty six characters this is the shortest thing in the month, and it earns its place only as the genuine opening line of the book, which is exactly the fame signal rule 2 allows.
